topComments.text: > How to run shell commands in parallel while limiting their concurrency. Depending upon the task, generate a Makefile and run it with: make -j <concurrency> > My original use case had to do with making a large number of web requests This is in fact the use case that caused me to think about using a Makefile for concurrency probably 20 years ago. A rule for downloading each URL to a file. Then a simple `make -j <jobs>` with whatever concurrency I desired and bonus: automatically skipping already downloaded files. To emulate one of the examples in the blog post: SHELL := bash .SHELLFLAGS := -o pipefail -c N := 1 2 3 4 5 REQS := $(N:%=req-%) .PHONY: all $(REQS) all: $(REQS) $(REQS): req-%: @curl -sS --fail-with-body --max-time 10 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"request": $*}' https://postman-echo.com/post | jq -c .json Run with: $ make -O -j 3 > If you know all commands that you want to execute up-front, then the solution gets far simpler. Ah, yeah, that does require something more clever than Make.

CREATE DATABASE sensor_quality_report; USE sensor_quality_report; CREATE TABLE readings(device STRING TAG,value DOUBLE FIELD); INSERT INTO readings(time,device,value) VALUES (1000,'probe_a',1.0),(2000,'probe_a','NaN'),(3000,'probe_a',-1.0); These two filters differ only by the additional ordinary value: SELECT time,value FROM readings WHERE value IN(CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)) ORDER BY time; SELECT time,value FROM readings WHERE value IN(CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE),1.0) ORDER BY time; +----+-----+ |time|value| +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +-----------------------------+-----+ | time|value| +-----------------------------+-----+ |1970-01-01T08:00:01.000+08:00| 1.0| |1970-01-01T08:00:02.000+08:00| NaN| +-----------------------------+-----+ The two-item query returns both 1.0 and NaN ; the one-item query returns no rows. infoqArticles.description: Google has open-sourced AQuA, a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source snapshots. In a 32-session replay, developers reduced seat selection bypasses from 15 sessions to two and dietary preference omissions from seven to zero after prompt changes. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Netflix Turns Operational Data Into a Knowledge Graph for AI-Driven Observability

infoqArticles.description: Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. By Henry Wilson
infoqArticles.author: Henry Wilson

infoqArticles.title: Podcast: Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary
infoqArticles.description: In this podcast, Shane Hastie, Lead Editor for Culture & Methods, spoke to Hugo Venturini about who is accountable when AI writes the code, how AI is reshaping code review and traditional engineering roles, and how leaders build a culture of transparency and psychological safety. infoqArticles.author: Hugo Venturini

infoqArticles.title: Dropbox Shares How Its In-House Cookie Auditor Tests Consent Behaviour Across 200+ Web Surfaces
infoqArticles.description: Dropbox engineers described a Playwright-based auditor that checks cookie consent behavior across more than 200 web surfaces. It runs three tests per page: US visitor, EU visitor, and Global Privacy Control signal. Cookie rules are kept outside the code. A companion tool finds live URLs. Weekly reports separate likely violations from false positives. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing
infoqArticles.description: Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. infoqArticles.author: Ben Linders

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector

infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript

Its author built it after duplicated validators drifted apart across web and mobile. It validates and formats data only, and does not process payments. He is cautious about adding SEPA and ACH file generation. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis
